blocks.text: Fourth, eagles in Scripture are sometimes great kings. Thus in Ezech. XVII, 3. A great eagle, with great wings, long pinions, full of feathers, of various colours, is the king of Babylon, as the same prophet explains in verse twelve. Again, in verse seven, A great eagle, with great wings and many feathers is the king of Egypt, on the interpretation of the same prophet in verse fifteen. And the reason for the likeness is obvious to everyone. For the eagle is powerful in strength, excels in swiftness, is keen of sight and fearless of spirit, and in the whole bearing of its body displays a certain royal majesty. Hence it is believed to hold dominion over the birds, as was proved at length at the beginning of this book ^{b)}. And the Persian kings had a golden eagle with outspread wings as their royal standard, as we have shown elsewhere from Xenophon, Curtius and Philostratus. Nor is it unlikely that the ancient kings of Assyria had this same standard, and that Scripture alludes to it whenever it designates them by the name of eagles: as in the words of Ezekiel just cited, A great eagle, etc.; and Dan. VII, 4., where it is said of the first beast, which foreshadowed the Babylonian empire, And it had the wings of an eagle; and Os. VIII, 1. The trumpet to your throat (say, set it there), As an eagle (he swoops) upon the house of the Lord. Here the Chaldee paraphrast has: O prophet, cry out with your throat as with a trumpet, and say, Behold! like an eagle that moves itself to and fro, so shall the king (of Assyria, Nebuchadnezzar) go up with his army, and encamp against the house of the sanctuary of the Lord. And Ierem. XLVIII, 40. As an eagle he has swooped, and he shall spread out his wings over the Moabites. And Ierem. XLIX, 22. He shall go up as an eagle, and swoop, and spread out his wings over Botsra. That is, like an eagle he rushed with force upon the prey before him, and brought his wars to an end with marvellous speed. And Ezekiel rightly calls that eagle great, because Nebuchadnezzar was a most powerful king; and he assigns him great wings, that is, great armies. As in Es. VIII, 8. His wings shall fill the breadth of your land. Wings, that is, forces. These things, indeed, the Egyptian king had in common with the Assyrian. So the Egyptian too is called a great eagle and with great wings. But the Assyrian had longer pinions and of more colours, that is, a greater dominion, extending over more [col. 185] peoples. And accordingly Ezekiel ascribes the length and variety of the pinions to him as his own. Note in passing that, like the Persian and Roman commanders of old, the Greeks also had the eagle as a military standard, if we believe Seneca in the Thebaid, where he says of the seven commanders at Thebes, in verse 389:

— — — now the bronze trumpets stir up war, and the eagle, as standard-bearer, set in motion, calls to battle. [II, 770] Fifth, the Chaldeans and Assyrians who, under the leadership of Nebuchadnezzar, laid waste all Judaea, levelled Jerusalem to the ground and consumed the temple with fire, are often compared by the Prophets to eagles hastening to their food and swooping upon their prey. See Ier. IV, 13. Thren. IV, 19. Hab. I, 8. Therefore these threats of the law also refer to them, Deut. XXVIII, 49. The Lord will raise up against you a distant nation, which will swoop like an eagle from the furthest ends of the earth. And Baal Hatturim is mistaken in referring this to Alexander, relying on a futile reason, namely that the Prophet's words ידאה הנשר, that is, the eagle will swoop, are ἰσόψηφοι [isopsēphoi] with the word עשרה, that is, ten; and Alexander completed a ten days' march in one day. But after the death of Nebuchadnezzar those eagle's wings of the Assyrians were gradually plucked off, as Daniel VII, 4. had foretold, and their empire was utterly overthrown by the Persians.
